new_statements.quote: El ZOCO presenta un tipo de acento con patrón trocaico (fuerte-débil), no privilegia bases o morfemas, y además no es sensible al peso de las sílabas porque pueden ser ligeras (CV) o pesadas (CVC), como se muestran en (1). Cuando las palabras son monosilábicas, entonces la única sílaba es la que lleva el acento, como en los ejemplos de (2). (1) a. [ꞌtu.wiʔ] 'perro' b. [ꞌkuh.ʃuʔts] ... [ꞌσ.σ] ... El patrón silábico trocaico se marca de derecha a izquierda como se nota en las palabras trisilábicas en (3), y en las de cuatro sílabas, como en (4). (3) a. [kə.ꞌca.hu] 'pasaron' b. [mi.ꞌduʔ.am] 'ya vino' [σ.ꞌσ.σ] (4) a. [poʔk.ʃa.ꞌhu.ʔam] 'Ya se sentaron' b. [kuj.kiʔm.ꞌpa.bə] 'El que se sube en el árbol' [σ.σ.ꞌσ.σ]
new_statements.translation: Ocotepec Zoque (ZOCO) has a trochaic (strong-weak) stress pattern; it does not privilege bases or morphemes, and it is not sensitive to syllable weight, since [stressed] syllables may be light (CV) or heavy (CVC), as shown in (1). When words are monosyllabic, the only syllable carries the stress, as in (2). ... The trochaic pattern is assigned from right to left, as seen in trisyllabic words in (3) and four-syllable words in (4) [all with stress on the penultimate syllable].
new_statements.citation: de la Cruz Morales, Román. 2023. Las clases de palabras mayores y menores en el zoque de Ocotepec, Chiapas. Tesis de doctorado en Lingüística Indoamericana, Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (CIESAS), Ciudad de México.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (CIESAS/INPI doctoral thesis, title page 'Las clases de palabras mayores y menores en el zoque de Ocotepec, Chiapas', Román de la Cruz Morales, dir. Roberto Zavala, Nov 2023). extracted text of PDF p. 39 (printed p. 19, ch. 2 §2.2 'Rasgos polisintéticos', footnote 4 attached to example (1a)) contains the quoted prose word-for-word: 'El ZOCO presenta un tipo de acento con patrón trocaico (fuerte-débil), no privilegia bases o morfemas, y además no es sensible al peso de las sílabas porque pueden ser ligeras (CV) o pesadas (CVC), como se muestran en (1). Cuando las palabras son monosilábicas, entonces la única sílaba es la que lleva el acento, como en los ejemplos de (2).' followed by (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (morphologically complex) word: a single right-aligned, weight-insensitive trochee, counting suffixes and enclitics (e.g. =pə REL, -ʔam 'ya') as part of the stress domain; monosyllables are stressed. Faarlund 2012 (snippets) states the same rule ('regularly on the penultimate syllable... regardless whether the stressed syllable belongs to the root or to a suffix or a clitic') and adds two morphophonological exceptions yielding final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by de la Cruz Morales 2023. Second-hand (Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody 2021 snippet, citing Herrera Zendejas 1993 and Faarlund 2012): secondary stress on every other syllable preceding the primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: de la Cruz Morales: none. Faarlund 2012 (snippet only): (1) plural -yaj + dependent -e/i contracts to -yé, stressed even when word-final (mye'ché 'searching', chükyé 'making'); (2) plural -tam + -u contraction leaves stress on the a. Harrison & Harrison 1984: Spanish-loan compounds carry a written accent because they deviate; Zoque-Zoque compounds keep a main stress on each member.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes and enclitics (examples (4a,b) show enclitic =pə and -ʔam counted for penult placement); examples are inflected verb forms and nouns in citation/utterance form from a text corpus.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (de la Cruz Morales 2023) and Faarlund 2012 both describe the Ocotepec/Tapalapa variety ('zoque de Ocotepec', ZOCO; Faarlund: 'Ocotepec/Tapalapa variant of Chiapas Zoque'), which Glottolog Harrison & Harrison 1984 is the Rayón town variety proper; Herrera Zendejas 1995 describes Chapultenango Zoque, also within the zor area. All sources examined agree or are consistent with penultimate stress; no dialect-internal disagreement seen.

sources.citation: Harrison, Roy y Margaret B. de Harrison (comps.); Francisco López Juárez y Cosme Ordoñes (colabs. zoques). 1984. Vocabulario zoque de Rayón. (Serie de diccionarios y vocabularios indígenas 'Mariano Silva y Aceves' 28.) México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. xiii+113 pp.
sources.note: Front matter 'El acento y el guión', p. xiii (PDF p. 14): written accent is used only on Spanish+Zoque compound words that would otherwise be mispronounced (ánima-jos, giniádʌjk); Zoque-Zoque compounds keep 'un acento principal en cada parte'. No explicit rule for where native word stress falls (implies it is predictable).
